rmt-2007-adv-01.title: Determinant zero
rmt-2007-adv-01.body:
A homogeneous system has a nonzero solution exactly when the determinant is $0$.

$\det=1(3k-16)-2(k-12)+2(4-9)=k-2$.

So $k=2$.

**Answer: 2**

rmt-2007-adv-01.title: Dependent rows
rmt-2007-adv-01.body:
Take $5\cdot(\text{row }1)-2\cdot(\text{row }2)=(3,4,2)$. So if $k=2$ the third row is a combination of the first two, the system has only two independent equations in three unknowns, and a nonzero solution exists. For other $k$ the rows are independent.

**Answer: 2**

rmt-2007-adv-02.title: Change to base 7 and base 3
rmt-2007-adv-02.body:
$\log_3 27=3$, $\log_x7=\frac1{\log_7x}$, $\log_{27}x=\frac13\log_3x$ and $\log_3x\cdot\log_73=\log_7x$.

Let $u=\log_7x$. The equation becomes $\frac{3}{u}=\frac13\log_3x\cdot\frac1{\log_37}$, and $\log_3x/\log_37=\log_7x=u$, so $\frac3u=\frac u3$, i.e. $u^2=9$.

Thus $\log_7x=\pm3$ and $x=343$ or $x=\frac1{343}$. The least is $\frac1{343}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{343}$**

rmt-2007-adv-03.title: Count paths
rmt-2007-adv-03.body:
All paths: $\binom94=126$. Paths through $(2,3)$: $\binom52$ ways to reach it times $\binom42$ ways to go on, $10\cdot6=60$.

Probability $=\frac{60}{126}=\frac{10}{21}$.

**Answer: $\frac{10}{21}$**

rmt-2007-adv-04.title: Track truthfulness
rmt-2007-adv-04.body:
If $k$ is not a square, $P_k$ and $P_{k+1}$ are the same type (both truthful or both liars). If $k$ is a square, they are of opposite types. So the type flips exactly at each perfect square $k\le n$ as we go around the circle.

Going all the way around from $P_1$ back to $P_1$ must flip the type an even number of times. The number of perfect squares in $1,\dots,n$ is $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$, so $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$ must be even.

For $n>1000$: $31^2=961<1000<1024=32^2$, and $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor=31$ is odd for $1001\le n\le1023$. The first $n$ with an even floor is $n=1024$.

**Answer: 1024**

rmt-2007-adv-05.title: Recursion
rmt-2007-adv-05.body:
Let $g(n)$ be the minimum. To move the bottom disk, the top $n-1$ disks must first be on the third peg ($g(n-1)$ moves at least), then the bottom disk moves, then those $n-1$ disks must be moved on top of it (another $g(n-1)$). So $g(n)\ge 2g(n-1)+1$, and this is achieved. With $g(1)=1$ we get $g(n)=2g(n-1)+1$, so $g(n)+1=2(g(n-1)+1)$ and $g(n)=2^n-1$.

**Answer: $2^n-1$**

rmt-2007-adv-07.title: Insert the largest element
rmt-2007-adv-07.body:
Build a permutation of length $n$ by inserting $n$ into a permutation of length $n-1$ (which has $n$ possible slots).

Start from a permutation with $k$ ascents. Inserting $n$ at the very front, or in the middle of one of the $k$ ascents (between $a_i<a_{i+1}$), keeps the number of ascents at $k$: that is $k+1$ slots. So $a=k+1$.

Start from a permutation with $k-1$ ascents. It has $n-2-(k-1)=n-k-1$ descents. Inserting $n$ at the very end, or inside a descent, creates one extra ascent: $1+(n-k-1)=n-k$ slots. So $b=n-k$.

**Answer: $(k+1,\;n-k)$**

rmt-2007-adv-08.title: Lower bound and construction
rmt-2007-adv-08.body:
Pegs only move toward the other side. Each red peg must advance $n+1$ holes and so must each blue peg, for a total of $2n(n+1)$ holes of advance. A slide advances one hole; a jump advances two holes. Each red peg must pass each blue peg exactly once, and each pass is done by a jump of one of the two pegs, so there are at least $n^2$ jumps and at most $n^2$ of them can save a move. Hence the number of moves is at least $2n(n+1)-n^2=n^2+2n$.

This is achieved: alternate moves so that no two pegs of the same color are adjacent when they need to move (slide a red, jump with a blue, slide a blue, ...). After $1+2+\dots+n$ moves the pegs alternate with the gap at one end; then $n$ jumps send the gap to the other end, and the symmetric procedure takes another $n+(n-1)+\dots+1$ moves. The total is $n(n+1)+n=n^2+2n$.

**Answer: $n^2+2n$**

rmt-2007-adv-08.title: Check small cases
rmt-2007-adv-08.body:
A breadth-first search of all board positions gives $3$ moves for $n=1$, $8$ for $n=2$, $15$ for $n=3$ and $24$ for $n=4$, matching $n^2+2n$.

**Answer: $n^2+2n$**

rmt-2007-adv-09.title: Write the equations
rmt-2007-adv-09.body:
Let $a=b^2$ and $X=\begin{pmatrix}u&v\\y&z\end{pmatrix}$. Then $X^2=aI$ means $u^2+vy=a$, $yv+z^2=a$, $(u+z)v=0$, $(u+z)y=0$.

**Case $u+z\equiv0$.** Then $z=-u$ and the only condition is $u^2+vy=a$. For each $u$: if $u^2\ne a$ (that is $p-2$ values of $u$), $vy=a-u^2\neq0$ has $p-1$ solutions $(v,y)$; if $u=\pm b$, $vy=0$ has $2p-1$ solutions. Total: $(p-2)(p-1)+2(2p-1)=p^2+p$.

**Case $u+z\not\equiv0$.** Then $v=y=0$, so $u^2=z^2=a$, i.e. $u,z\in\{\pm b\}$ with $u\ne -z$, so $u=z=\pm b$: 2 matrices ($\pm bI$).

Total: $p^2+p+2$.

**Answer: $p^2+p+2$**

rmt-2007-adv-09.title: Check
rmt-2007-adv-09.body:
A direct count for $p=3$ gives $14=3^2+3+2$ and for $p=5$ gives $32=5^2+5+2$.

**Answer: $p^2+p+2$**

rmt-2007-adv-10.title: Only neighbours can give primes
rmt-2007-adv-10.body:
$P(a)-P(b)$ is a sum of terms $c_k(a^k-b^k)$, each divisible by $a-b$, so $a-b$ divides $P(a)-P(b)$. Moreover, the quotient $\frac{P(a)-P(b)}{a-b}$ is a sum of positive terms and is greater than $1$ because the degree is large and all numbers are positive. So $|P(a)-P(b)|$ can be prime only if $|a-b|=1$. In the worst case every pair of consecutive integers in $T$ gives a prime (and these primes are all different, since $P(a+1)-P(a)$ is increasing). So $T$ may contain at most $6$ pairs of consecutive integers.

Let $T$ have $e\le6$ such pairs and consist of $r$ blocks of consecutive integers; then $|T|=e+r$. The blocks are separated by at least one missing number, so $|T|+(r-1)\le2007$, i.e. $e+2r\le2008$ and $r\le1001$ for $e=6$. Hence $|T|\le6+1001=1007$.

This is attained: take all odd numbers $1,3,\dots,2007$ (1004 numbers, no neighbours) and add three even numbers, each of which creates two neighbouring pairs, giving $1007$ elements and exactly $6$ pairs.

**Answer: 1007**
